passages.happening: Moses speaks to the heads of the tribes. “This is what the LORD has commanded: If a man makes a vow to the LORD or swears an oath to obligate himself by a pledge, he must not break his word; he must do everything he has promised” (verses 1-2).
passages.hearers:
The calendar of chapters 28 and 29 ended by mentioning vows, the gifts individuals promised to God over and above the nation's offerings. This chapter takes them up.

A vow was a promise made to God. People in the ancient world made them often, and so did Israel. A person in danger, in sickness, childless or going to war would promise something to God if he would help. Jacob vowed a tenth of all he had if God brought him home (Genesis 28:20-22). Hannah vowed that if God gave her a son, she would give the boy back to him (1 Samuel 1:11).

The chapter uses two words. A vow, neder, was usually a promise to give or to do something. A pledge, issar, comes from a Hebrew root that means to bind, and seems to mean a promise to go without something. Both were spoken aloud, and once spoken they were binding.

The rule for a man is given in one sentence. He must not break his word. A word given to God is a serious thing, and it is to be kept in full.

The law is addressed to the heads of the tribes. They judged disputes among their clans, and questions about vows would come to them.

Underneath the rule is a belief about God. Israel's God keeps his word. This book has just spent three chapters showing that he will not go back on his promise, even when a king pays for it. People who belong to such a God are to be people whose word can be relied on.
passages.later:
The wisdom books warn against vows made lightly: “When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it, because He takes no pleasure in fools. Fulfill your vow. It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it” (Ecclesiastes 5:4-5). And Proverbs says, “It is a trap for a man to dedicate something rashly, only later to reconsider his vows” (Proverbs 20:25).

Jesus took the matter further. He taught his followers to be so truthful that they need no oaths at all: “Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37).
passages.asks: A promise made to God was to be kept in full. Ask what you have promised God, in a crisis or in a moment of gratitude, and then let slide. And ask whether your ordinary yes and no can be relied on by the people who hear them.

passages.t: The vows of daughters and wives
passages.happening:
The law then turns to women, in four cases.

A young woman still in her father's house makes a vow. If her father hears of it and says nothing, it stands. “But if her father prohibits her on the day he hears about it, then none of the vows or pledges by which she has bound herself shall stand. The LORD will absolve her because her father has prohibited her” (verse 5).

A woman marries while under a vow. Her husband may cancel it when he first hears of it (verses 6-8).

“Every vow a widow or divorced woman pledges to fulfill is binding on her” (verse 9).

A married woman makes a vow in her husband's house. If he says nothing, it stands. If he cancels it on the day he hears, it does not, ‘and the LORD will absolve her’ (verse 12). “But if he nullifies them after he hears of them, then he will bear her iniquity” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
A modern reader notices at once that this law does not treat women and men alike. That is true, and it should be said plainly before anything else.

The law belongs to the households of ancient Israel. A household was headed by a man, first the father and after marriage the husband. He was answerable for its property and its living. And a vow usually involved property: an animal for sacrifice, a gift to the sanctuary, a time of going without food. A daughter's or wife's vow could commit what belonged to the whole household. So the law gave its head a say.

The law does not create that kind of household. It finds it, as it finds it everywhere in that world, and it sets limits inside it. Four of those limits are worth seeing.

The man must act at once. He may cancel the vow only ‘on the day he hears about it’. He cannot keep his objection in reserve and bring it out later to hold over her.

Silence counts as consent. If he says nothing, the vow stands, and he cannot afterward pretend he never agreed (verse 14).

The woman is cleared. If her vow is cancelled, ‘the LORD will absolve her’. She is not left guilty before God for a promise she was prevented from keeping.

The man answers for misuse. If he lets the vow stand and later forces her to break it, the guilt is his: ‘he will bear her iniquity’.

Then there is verse 9, which is easy to pass over. A widow or a divorced woman has no man over her household, and her word binds her exactly as a man's binds him. The law does not think a woman's promise to God worth less than a man's, or think her less able to make one. Where she heads her own house, she answers for her own word.

Notice also what the chapter takes for granted throughout. Women made vows. They spoke to God for themselves, without a priest or a husband between. Hannah's vow, made alone at the sanctuary in great distress, is one of the best-known prayers in the Old Testament, and her husband let it stand.
passages.later:
When Hannah told her husband Elkanah what she had vowed, he answered, “Do what you think is best” (1 Samuel 1:23). The vow stood, and her son Samuel was given to the LORD.

Paul writes that in Christ ‘there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus’ (Galatians 3:28).
passages.hard:
Why can a father or husband cancel a woman's vow, when no one can cancel a man's? And does this give a husband or father authority over a woman's faith today?

The chapter reflects the household of its time, in which the father or husband was its legal and economic head. Because vows often committed the household's goods, he was given the right to review them. The law does not treat men and women the same, and a reader is right to notice.

Christians respond to this in different ways. Some stress that the law assumes the order of its world and does not command it, and that the Bible's story moves toward a fuller statement of the equal standing of men and women (Galatians 3:28). Others read the law as setting out real responsibilities within a household that still carry meaning. Many point out, on either view, how far the chapter goes to limit the man's power and to protect the woman's conscience. These notes take no side between those readings.

One thing can be said without hesitation. This was a law about vows of goods and of fasting in the households of ancient Israel. It is not a rule for any husband's or father's control of a woman today. It gives no man the right to decide what a woman may believe, how she may pray, whether she may worship, what she may give, or what she may promise God. A man who uses Scripture to control a woman's conscience, her money or her movements is misusing it.

If you are being pressured or forced in your marriage, it is not your fault, and these verses do not ask you to submit to it. Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The law required a man to speak at once or not at all, and laid the guilt on him if he misused his say. Ask where you hold power over another person's choices, in a family or at work, and whether you use it promptly, openly and for their good. And ask whether you treat the promises that other people make to God as theirs to keep.
